items.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: when I first heard Charles Mingus on a record, he was doing something I had never heard music do before.

ctx.x: I’m wondering if, because of so much education going on with jazz now that we’ve dissected everything they do and there is so much for people to copy that that’s how they end up.

Well that’s the institutionalization, that’s what I meant by it’s good on one hand — I mean it preserves what they’ve done in a way, which I think is good. But the methodology and the thinking process for acquiring the knowledge — and I think that this music really is a different kind of, you know I think it really requires a different type of education. The standards, the rules, the things to get the spirit and the essence of the music is different than what the institutions, the kinds of rules that apply to…
Right. You’ve got a lot of different projects going on right now. You are doing some Latin music I see?

items.title: 67802_Charles Mingus oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Yeah, sure. Have you heard Chico Freeman? ... [INTERVIEWEE] A player should be an actor, a great actor.

ctx.x: It should have all that in it.
Yeah, sure. Have you heard Chico Freeman? He's (inaudible) go in and out.
A player should be an actor, a great actor. I mean, one that makes you cry on certain roles.
